Juvenile Louisiana pigtoe mussels experience a critical developmental milestone during larval settlement, at which point the shell length is a mere 0.03 centimeters . Following this benthic transition, the newly metamorphosed individuals must locate suitable gravel substrates to begin their sessile existence. The initial shell dimensions at the moment of birth, when the glochidia are released from the marsupial gills of the gravid female, have been recorded at 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], an extremely small size indicative of a parasitic larval stage. This early ontogenetic phase is brief, with the age at birth occurring only 10 days [ab = 10 days] after egg fertilization, when the water temperature is held at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The protracted development of this freshwater unionid reflects the energetic constraints of its environment, and field surveys consistently report that the ultimate shell length attained by adults in stable populations of the Neches River basin reaches approximately 6.8 centimeters [Li = approximately 6.8 centimeters], a size that is modest in comparison to other members of the Pleurobema genus.

Sexual maturation in Pleurobema riddellii is achieved once individuals reach a shell length of 3.76 centimeters [Lp = 3.76 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity for reproductive effort. Reaching this size requires several years of continuous filter feeding on fine particulate organic matter. Upon attaining this pubertal size, the mussels become reproductively active adults capable of brooding glochidia within their demibranchs. The timing of reproductive activity is tightly coupled to thermal conditions; at a consistent temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females produce approximately 50.4 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 50.4 offspring per day], a rate derived from gravid individuals measured at a shell length of 4.31 centimeters. This energetic investment is considerable, as each brood cycle demands substantial metabolic resources for the development of parasitic larvae that must later attach to a suitable fish host. The species typically spawns once during the late spring and early summer months, a strategy that synchronizes larval release with the seasonal activity of darters and other potential host fishes.

The maximum lifespan of the Louisiana pigtoe under natural conditions has been estimated at an estimated 7300 days [am = an estimated 7300 days] when individuals are maintained at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This longevity is relatively protracted for a unionid of modest adult size, reflecting a life history strategy characterized by delayed senescence and low natural mortality in undisturbed habitats. The ability to persist for such an extended duration allows for multiple reproductive events across several decades. A gravid individual with a shell length of 5.1 centimeters achieves a total wet weight of 14.4 grams [Wwi = 14.4 grams], a body mass that reflects the accumulation of gonadal tissue and somatic growth necessary for supporting repeated brooding cycles. This weight is quite substantial compared to the larval mass at birth, underscoring the considerable biomass gain accomplished over the mussels ontogeny. Age-related death in this species is typically preceded by a gradual decline in filtration efficiency and metabolic function.

Comparative analyses with the closely related Pleurobema strodeanum provide valuable context for understanding the reproductive biology of the Louisiana pigtoe. The daily reproductive output observed at a shell length of 4.31 centimeters, equating to roughly 50.4 offspring per day [Ri = roughly 50.4 offspring per day] under stable thermal conditions, has prompted ecologists to investigate the trade-offs between brooding duration and larval quality. The early life stages of this species are particularly vulnerable, with a shell length at settlement of only 0.03 centimeters  highlighting the fragility of newly recruited individuals as they transition from a parasitic existence on fish gills to a free-living benthic juvenile. The minute glochidial birth size of 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] makes them challenging to detect in plankton tows and drift samples, complicating efforts to quantify recruitment success and population connectivity across fragmented riverine habitats. Conservation efforts must therefore account for these microscopic life stages when assessing the viability of imperiled populations.

Population modeling of this species benefits from precise demographic parameters, including the size at puberty of 3.76 centimeters [Lp = 3.76 centimeters]. A significant proportion of adult mortality occurs immediately following the reproductive season, when individuals are energetically depleted and more susceptible to predation by muskrats and raccoons. The maximum lifespan is recorded at approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] under optimal conditions, consistent with a strategy that prioritizes gradual growth toward the ultimate shell length of 6.8 centimeters [Li = 6.8 centimeters] before allocating resources to multiple reproductive cycles at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Tissue mass accumulation progresses steadily throughout the sub-adult phase, and a shell length of 5.1 centimeters corresponds to a total wet weight of 14.4 grams [Wwi = 14.4 grams]. The larval phase remains an ephemeral window in the life cycle, with an age at birth of 10 days [ab = 10 days] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] dictating the window of opportunity for host fish infection. These fundamental measurements are essential for constructing stage-based projection matrices that inform recovery plans for this federally endangered species.
